outcome.description: You sweep the area with every sensor you have. The results come back empty. Not a scrap of wreckage, not a residual energy reading, nothing to explain what you saw. But your nav computer logs a curious detail: the ghost contact was broadcasting a Guild transponder code that was decommissioned two weeks ago. Sato's code. Someone is either using her identity or her ship survived. Either way, someone wants you to notice.

Your diagnostics come back clean: every system nominal. The contact was real, or at least your sensors believed it was. You log the anomaly and file it with the growing list of things that don't add up.
You adjust course. The sensor ghost fades behind you, just like the distress signal did.
You maneuver through the debris field, snagging intact crates with your cargo grapple. A few are damaged, but most contain sellable goods.
You plot a course around the floating junk and continue on your way.
You spend time chasing the signal. Turns out it was a chunk of ice sublimating near a heat vent. The chase leaves your sensors better calibrated.
You log the anomaly and move on. Your nav computer files it under 'unexplained readings', a list that grows longer every week.

You creep through at quarter thrust, sensors on full sweep. It takes the better part of an hour, but you emerge on the other side with hull intact and a detailed minefield map that salvage teams would pay for.
You plot a wide arc around the minefield. It costs you time.

You snag the tumbling pod and crack it open. Inside, a shivering engineer blinks in the sudden light. She was aboard a mining vessel that broke apart three days ago. She transfers her emergency fund and asks for a ride to the nearest station.
You match the pod's tumble and lock a power umbilical onto its hull. The batteries drink in the charge, and the beacon flares back to full strength. A rescue vessel should pick it up within hours.

No survivors. You find cargo containers stamped with Commerce Guild seals. All empty, contents transferred to whoever did this. One hull fragment still has a name visible: Patience of Kaur. A registered Guild freighter. The attack was recent enough that the metal is still warm in places. You take what you can and leave fast.
You run a fast sweep: three ship IDs, weapon signature profiles, debris age estimates. Enough for a report. You don't linger.
You plot a wide detour around the field. It costs time and fuel.

You transfer credits to the collection box. A second recording activates: 'Thank you for supporting the arts. As a patron, you are entitled to name one piece in the collection. Please transmit your title now.' You look at a twisted spire of antenna fragments reaching toward distant stars and transmit a title. The beacon logs your submission alongside hundreds of others. Apparently, seventeen different people have named pieces 'My Ex.' One is titled 'Tax Return.'

You cut engines to a drift and weave through the installation. Up close, the pieces tell stories: a children's toy welded to a warship hull plate, a wedding ring fused into a navigation console, a row of boots from six different stations arranged in a line like they're walking somewhere together. Tucked in the center, you find a small plaque: 'Everything out here was something to someone. T.W.' You emerge on the other side.
You run a materials scan. There's a decent haul of recyclable alloys in there. You mark the coordinates in your nav log. The light catches a child's drawing etched into a fuel cell casing.

Forty-seven names. Engineers, geologists, demolitions experts, medics. The youngest was nineteen. The oldest, sixty-three. Eleven of them share the same surname: Vasquez. A family that came to the Expanse together and went into the rock together. A note at the bottom reads: 'They built the floor we stand on.' You copy the manifest to your personal log.

You dock your auxiliary line and feed power into the buoy's aging cell. The display brightens, the names sharpen. As you disengage, your comms pick up a brief transmission from a nearby mining barge: 'Appreciate that, pilot. My grandmother's name is on that list.' The connection closes before you can respond.
You dip your running lights as you pass, the spacer's salute. The memorial shrinks behind you, a small point of light among millions. But this one was placed on purpose.

The seal breaks with a hiss of preserved atmosphere: air from Earth, a hundred and fifty years stale. Inside: letters, hundreds of them, handwritten on paper that crumbles at the edges. Drawings by children. Photographs printed on polymer sheets. A pressed flower, impossibly fragile, that disintegrates when the vacuum touches it. One letter, written in a steady hand, reads: 'We are sending you everything we couldn't carry. Not cargo. Memory. Remember rain. Remember birdsong. Remember that the sky was blue. Build something worthy of what we lost.' You seal the container and store it.

You secure the capsule in your cargo bay without breaking the seal. You file a recovery report and tag the capsule as historical material. The archivist who responds sounds like they might be crying. 'We've been looking for the missing pods for decades. Thank you. Thank you.'
You log the coordinates and leave the capsule to its drift. The letters inside will continue their long, silent orbit: words from the dead, waiting for readers who may never come.

You spend an hour scooping titanium clusters back into Britt's remaining bays. She's efficient and grateful without being sentimental about it. 'You just saved my quarterly bonus. Here. Take a share. Fair's fair.' She splits the salvage evenly.
You grab what's drifted beyond Britt's recovery range. She watches on sensors but doesn't say anything.
You plot a course around the glittering cloud. Britt's voice follows you out: 'Smart flying. Stay safe out there.' The titanium catches the starlight behind you like a scattered constellation.

You burn hard toward the engagement zone, weapons hot. The pirates, not expecting reinforcements, break off their grapple runs and scatter. They're fast enough to escape, but they leave half the cargo pods behind. The Solidarity's captain, a veteran named Fen Okoro, sends you a share of the recovered titanium's value. "Breakstone remembers its friends, Captain. Every shift, every shaft."
You hold back and watch the pirates strip the hauler. When they jump out, you move in and collect three cargo pods they missed. The Solidarity's captain sees you on sensors and says nothing.
You adjust your heading to give the engagement a wide berth. The Solidarity's distress call echoes on your comms as you pull away.
